description:
We are a group of students from Seville heavily interested on Mathematics and Computer Science. Even though we are only in our first year of college, we are passionate about space, data analysis and computer algorithms to solve the complex problems that will shape the future.

So, as a wise man once said:

‘Empieza el rock and roll’
summary:
We developed Maia, a navigation assistant for Mars that is simple to use and works with no internet at all. Once set up, everything runs on a local server, so it keeps working when communications with Earth are delayed or down, exactly when an astronaut needs it most.

Maia is built to be easy under real conditions. Astronauts just speak to her instead of typing, which is difficult in pressurized gloves. For each trip she offers three routes colored like a traffic light by risk: green is safe, yellow is moderate, red is risky. The clean interface is made to be understood at a glance, not a cryptic 2D map with more information than anyone can process in a dangerous situation. Travel times come from a real digital elevation model and the specs of existing Mars rovers, and astronauts can add their own points to the map.

Because Maia is fully local, it could run on small hardware, even a smartwatch, and help an astronaut get back to base when there is no connection. Built with Docker Compose, Ollama, Python, FastAPI, and React.

Limitations: The first run needs internet to download several GB of Docker images and speech data. After that, everything runs locally.
details:
What it does

Maia is a navigation assistant for Mars that works with no internet. We run it as a local server with Docker Compose, and it uses Ollama to host the language models on the device itself. You talk to Maia instead of typing, using the Web Speech API, and she runs the commands for you. That matters because typing in a pressurized glove is a pain.

Ask her for a route and you get three, colored like a traffic light by risk: green is the safe one, yellow is in the middle, red is the risky one. Travel time for each route is worked out from a starting point on a real digital elevation model, using the specs of rovers that already exist. Astronauts can also add their own points to the map. In the demo that only saves a location, but it’s the part we’re most curious to grow.

Why we built it this way

Mars doesn’t have an instant connection to Earth, so any tool that needs the internet is a tool that fails at the worst moment. We wanted something that keeps working when communications are down, and could help an astronaut get back to base. Since everything is local, it can run on small hardware, even something like a smartwatch.

Intended impact

We want astronauts to have one less thing to worry about when something goes wrong. The crew-added map points also mean the map gets better as people explore, without waiting on updates from Earth.

What we used

Docker Compose, Ollama with local models, and the Web Speech API. Python with fastAPI with networkX and ReactJS with threeJS in the frontend.

What’s creative about it

Most navigation tools assume you’re online. We started from the opposite assumption and built around it: a local assistant, voice control for gloved hands, and a risk system you can read at a glance. And we also wanted a beautiful UI, not a cryptic 2d map with more info than any human in a dangerous situation could process.

What we considered

No connectivity, hands that can’t type, the cost of picking a risky route, and hardware that may be very small. We also kept the crew-added data simple on purpose so it could be extended later.

IMPORTANT:

For now for the docker to start you have to be connected to the internet, but once it has started, everything is local, even though the local web speech API needs to run a first time online to download the en_US speech model on the browser.

Future work

  • Let astronauts attach more than a location to a map point, such as notes, hazards, photos, or terrain type, and have that feed back into the risk ratings.
  • Share map updates between devices over a local radio or mesh link, so a crew’s additions reach everyone without a connection to Earth.
  • Make so that the path can be reverse, meaning that the rovers could move towars the astronaut, like the Perseverance in the Jezero crater for example.
  • Test on actual low-power hardware, like wearables, and shrink the models to fit.
  • Add live inputs such as battery level, vehicle condition, and time left before dark, so the route suggestions respond to the situation.
  • Add more parts of mars in high resolution, like we have now with Jezero and Gale crates, and fix Valles Marineris.
